newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Bank supervisors start search for global standards.
newsitem.headline: Bank supervisors start search for global standards.

text.p: Banking supervisors from around the world will start developing global banking standards to prevent financial crises in the 21st century.

Expertise from the Group of 10 (G10) leading industrial nations and emerging and transition economies will be included in developing global banking standards to ensure every country's banks fit into the international scene.

G10 officials have debated plans for minimum banking standards in recent months, and monetary sources said the debate should pick up again at Monday's monthly meeting of G10 central bank governors at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).

The standards, part of the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) crisis prevention strategy, will be used as a form of micro surveillance in conjunction with enhanced surveillance of economies and tougher reporting criteria for economic data.

Though there is universal agreement on the need to reform some banking systems, supervisors caution there is no quick fix because the origins of crises are multiple and range from legal and political impediments to a volatile operating environment.
"Banking regulations are important, but secondary to monetary and fiscal policies. We should not confuse cause and effect," said one international economist.

The aggressive push to improve banking systems in emerging markets is mainly coming from the IMF and G7, where fears of a new crisis along the lines of Mexico's financial crisis in late 1994 runs very deep.
At a summit in Lyon, G7 leaders sought swift action to improve banking supervision in emerging economies and asked finance ministers to report back in Denver.
In July, Tommaso Padoa-Schioppa, chairman of the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision, briefed G10 central bankers on his plans to strengthen links to non-G10 countries.
His plans included creation of a working group comprised of G10 and non-G10 banking supervisors.

G10 deputies are coordinating a search for global banking standards as part of an international push to reform fragile banking systems. A progress report is expected to be presented at the Spring IMF meeting and the Group of Seven (G7) summit in Denver in June 1997.
IMF and World Bank experts are also hastily working on banking standards.
"Finance ministers want to see results. They may not understand banking supervision, but they don't really care. They just want it done," said one international financial source.

Michel Camdessus, managing director of IMF, has identified fragile national banking systems as the Achilles' heel of the global economy and suspects that the next international economic crises could begin in the banking sector.

But even if the next crisis comes from an external shock, the world's financial system is so integrated and capital flows so massive that a shake in fragile banking systems could transmit and amplify shocks and raise prospects of systemic risk, economists say.

Global banking standards, which could be recommendations for best banking practices, are likely to address a wide range of issues including capital adequacy, accounting and provisioning, insolvency and connected lending.
For example, banks operating in more volatile economic environments will likely have to fulfill higher capital standards than the Basle Accord's minimum risk-weighted eight percent.
Supervisors stress that the Basle Accord's capital adequacy ratios are a minimum and in the case of Mexico, the banks had fulfilled the eight-percent capital ratio.
But many of the issues to be addressed will be beyond the traditional scope of the G10-dominated Basle Committee.

"For such countries (emerging markets), the Basle rules may not provide sufficient support to the fulfilment of basic prerequisites for sound banking, or be too sophisticated and difficult to comply with, or disregard specific problems that are not acute in G10 economies," Padoa-Schioppa told the June international conference of banking supervisors.
Legal systems and standards for insider lending were also left aside to be covered by individual central banks or nations.
